questions.q: Why does the handler check `opp.StageName == 'Closed Won' && oldOpp.StageName != 'Closed Won'` instead of just `opp.StageName == 'Closed Won'`?
options: Checking the old value too ensures the Task is only created on the actual transition into Closed Won, not on every subsequent update to an already-closed-won Opportunity
Both conditions are equivalent; the second is redundant
Apex requires comparing against Trigger.oldMap in every after-update trigger
Without the old value check, the trigger would not compile
questions.explain: Comparing against Trigger.oldMap's previous StageName ensures the follow-up Task is created only once, exactly when the Opportunity newly transitions into Closed Won, not on every later edit to an already-closed-won record.

questions.q: Where does the handler issue its DML insert statement, and why does that placement matter?
options: Inside the for loop, once per matching Opportunity, for simplicity
In a separate scheduled job, never inside the trigger context
After the for loop ends, on the whole collected List<Task> at once, so exactly one DML statement runs regardless of batch size
DML is never issued; Tasks are created declaratively instead
questions.explain: Collecting Tasks into a List across the loop and inserting once after the loop keeps the DML statement count constant no matter how many Opportunities are in the trigger batch — the bulkification principle from Lesson 27.

questions.q: What does the `if (!followUpTasks.isEmpty())` guard before the insert accomplish?
options: It prevents the trigger from ever running on bulk updates
It deletes any existing Tasks first
It is required syntax with no functional effect
It avoids issuing an unnecessary DML statement when no Opportunity in this batch actually transitioned to Closed Won
questions.explain: Without this guard, an empty insert would still count as a DML statement; checking isEmpty() first avoids wasting a DML statement when there's genuinely nothing to insert.

questions.q: Why is the trigger handler class declared `with sharing` in this project?
options: with sharing is required syntax for all trigger handlers
So this automation deliberately respects the running user's sharing rules rather than acting with unrestricted system-mode access
with sharing makes the code run faster
without sharing is not a valid keyword in Apex
questions.explain: with sharing is a deliberate choice here, enforcing the running user's sharing model for this automation rather than defaulting to broader access.

questions.q: If a team wants to add a second, unrelated piece of Opportunity automation later, what does this lesson recommend?
options: Add the new logic to the same OpportunityTriggerHandler method (or handler class), keeping one trigger per object as taught in Lesson 22
Write a second trigger on Opportunity dedicated to the new automation
Rewrite the entire automation from scratch in a Flow instead
Disable the existing trigger before adding new logic
questions.explain: Per Lesson 22's one-trigger-per-object principle, new Opportunity automation should extend the existing handler rather than introducing a second trigger on the same object, to keep execution order predictable.
